com.h:
The PictureCharacterValidation action library contains actions that are specialized validation actions
that verify and adjust individual characters and their confidence within a field.
The actions perform type validation on the input data on a character by character basis. It can confirm that the text within
a field matches expected patterns such as "upper-case alpha, alpha, numeric, numeric, alpha" where the string
is expected to have characters that follow this pattern. A more specific example would be validation
of a social security number which must be in the format "nnn-nn-nnnn" where "n" is a number. The
action can return a simple true or false indicating if a pattern is matched. The action library
can also do additional manipulation such as lowering the confidence of incorrect characters
and automatically replacing failed characters with text from the alternate field text strings.
The characters with the lowered confidence will then be flagged to verification operators in
a verification panel. Client verification panels highlight individual characters that are low confidence.
The verification panel can also enforce the same type requirements on each character prevent
field validation from succeeding until the operator has corrected all of the issues within each field.
Picture strings improve and filter recognition
results, and are used to limit characters typed into that field during verify.
Some of the actions obtain the required character pattern from a DCO variable called
"PictureString". If the required
picture string is defined in the PictureString variable, then the verify panel will require
that a user's input also meet the requirement.
The
FormatPictureFields
and
FilterPictureFields
actions can be called to “enforce” the
specified PictureString after recognition rules are invoked. The ApplyPictureString action
is an exception that does not use the PictureString variable, instead the picture string
is passed as a parameter to the action.
Recognition actions do not use the PictureString property variable.
However, individual recognition engines have their own
parameters to help guide the recognition and can limit the characters
recognized for a field, providing hints to the engine as to what characters
are expected on the source page, improving recognition quality.
Refer to the settings for the engine you are using to recognize text.
If the recognized character set for a field can be restricted to a set of characters, for example
all numeric only, all alpha only, or all upper-case only, etc., then this will improve recognition
results for the field. Refer to the recognition best practices document for more information
and the recognition properties in the Zones tab of Datacap Studio.
The Web Verify task always enforces the PictureString setting for a field that has the variable defined.
Thick client Verify panels constructed by
autoform also enforces PictureString specifications, if it is defined.
The DCEdit control enforces the PictureString requirements in a thick client verification panel.
There are two typical ways that the picture values can be set in PictureString.
1.
Use the rrunner action rrSet in a ruleset. With this action, you can specify the PictureString
variable and set it to the desired value.
2.
In the Zones tab of Datacap Studio, right click on the desired field in the DCO hierarchy
and choose "Manage Variables".
Enter the new variable PictureString and set its value to the desired picture string characters.
Setting the variable in the SetupDCO can be more efficient than setting it at runtime.
See the help in the action library VoteUsingComparativeText for more information
regarding the use of alternative text within a field. Some actions in this library
will use the alternative text, if available, when picture string mismatches occur.
Picture Character Identifiers
Picture strings, as they are called, are created using single character identifiers that determine
the expected pattern. Each picture character identifier corresponds to a specific type, or set, of
characters. The character in that position is expected to match the type.
The following lists the picture character identifiers that are available for configuring the picture string actions:
A: Alphabetic characters only or a space. Numeric and/or punctuation characters are not valid.
a: Alphabetic, space and punctuation characters.
D: Dates. The dates must be expressed with numeric characters. You can delimit months, dates, and years with hyphens, periods, and forward slashes.
F: Float numbers, which are fractional numbers. To accommodate fractional values, this picture string allows you to
include both numbers and a period (for the decimal separator). The F character also allows minus signs to represent negative numbers.
f: Numeric and punctuation characters.
L: Lower-case alphabetic and space characters.
l: Lower-case alphabetic, space and punctuation characters.
N: Numeric characters only.
n: Upper-case alphabetic, numeric or space characters.
P: Punctuation and space characters.
T: Time values. These values are expressed in numbers with a colon. In addition, the characters P, M, and A are allowed to distinguish between morning and afternoon times, and colon characters are allowed to delimit hours, minutes, and seconds.
U: Upper-case alphabetic and space characters.
u: Upper-case alphabetic, space and punctuation characters.
X: Alphabetic, space and numeric characters.
x: Alphabetic, space, numeric and punctuation characters.
Z: Any character.
#: Numeric characters and the minus sign.
Additional custom picture characters can be defined if there are combinations of characters that are needed
which are not already covered by the provided identifiers.
SetPictureCharacters can be used to define up to 10 additional application specific picture character identifiers
at runtime, identified as 0 through 9. For example, if character can be only one of these characters: "QWERTY",
then a custom picture identifier can be created containing that set of characters. When the custom identifier
is used in a picture string, then the characters must match those provided in the custom set.
Verification panels will only validate characters using the built-in picture identifiers. Custom identifiers
are not used by the verification panels.
The text is validated for DCO field node objects. For more information about the Datacap hierarchy,
see the action help in the ApplicationObjects action library.
Smart Parameters
Parameters that use an "@" notation, such as "@X.xxxx", "@P.xxxx", "@STRING()", "@PILOT()", etc., are
known as "smart parameters". The data passed as a parameter to an action will be evaluated at runtime.
For example, "@X" is notation for accessing the current object. "@P" accesses the page object, which
could be the current object, or a parent object. Being evaluated at runtime, allows recognized data
or other batch specific data to be passed to actions or stored as metadata. A smart parameter such
as @DATE could be used to name export files based on the current date. Similar smart parameters
will retrieve the current batch ID, current batch directory, current operator ID, and more.
Smart parameters are a very powerful mechanism of getting data from other areas of the application and copying
it into a new location or passing it as a parameter to an action. It is recommended that the smart parameter
documentation is reviewed to understand the full capabilities available. The top-level help of the
ValidationAndTextAdjustments action library also has information about smart parameters. Some characters such
as +, \ and . also have special smart parameter meaning and may be interpreted as a smart parameter. This
can be controlled using smart parameter syntax.

method.name: ApplyPictureString
method.ap:
PictureString:
The picture string to validate the field.
Smart parameters are supported.
method.h:
Validates the current field using a PictureString as an argument.
Using the provided picture string, this action will test that each of the characters in the current field
meet the requirement of each picture character identifier.
The provided picture string must be the same length or shorter than the data
on the field for the test to pass. If the picture string is shorter, then the last character of the picture
string will be used to validate all remaining characters in the field.
Unlike FormatPictureFields, which uses the PictureString variable, ApplyPictureString
accepts the picture string as a parameter only.
SetPictureCharacters("0","01")
SetPictureCharacters("1","0123")
SetPictureCharacters("2","-./")
ApplyPictureString("0N21N2NN")
This example first creates custom picture strings for picture character identifiers "0", "1" and "2" that
have sets of allowed characters that are not available in the predefined character identifiers.
They are then used in the ApplyPictureString action to provide
tighter control on the allowed input. "0N21N2NN" format matches a typical 6 digit date specification
like "01/07/67". The first character must be only a 0 or 1. The second character can be any number,
the third character must be a standard date separator "-", "." or "/", etc.
Note that a value such as "01/07/1967" would also pass this test because if the field is longer than
the picture string, the last identifier will be used on all remaining characters. Likewise, "01/07/1967123"
would also pass the test. This can be further validated by using length restrictions on the field
using the text length validation actions in the ValidationsAndTextAdjustments action library.
ApplyPictureString("AN")
This example requires that the field text is at least 2 characters long. The first character must
be an alphabetic character or a space. The second character must be a number. If the field
is longer than 2 characters, then all subsequent characters must also be a number.
If the field is only 1 character long or is empty, then the validation will fail.
ApplyPictureString("@X.MyPictureString")
This example shows that the value of the picture string will be retrieved
from the DCO variable called "MyPictureString" on the current DCO node.
method.ret:
False,
if called at the wrong level, if the picture string is longer than the field value
or if the field fails the picture string validation. Otherwise,
True.
method.see:
Refer to the top-level help topic for the list of available picture character
identifiers that can be used to create a picture string.

method.name: FilterPictureFields
method.ap: None.
method.h:
Uses a picture string to validate the text in a field.
Replaces a character and adjusts the confidence based on the "PictureString" variable defined for the field.
Before calling this action, the variable "PictureString" must be defined in the DCO node for the field
which will be used for validating the field. The variable
can be defined for the node in the Setup DCO or set at runtime using an action like rrSet.
The action lowers the Confidence Rating of any character in a field that does not satisfy the Picture String's criteria
and replaces the problem character with a low confidence space. It is very similar to the FormatPictureFields action but
does not use alternative recognition characters. The picture string used to validate each field is not provided
to this action and instead must be defined in the PictureString variable. This allows each field
to have a unique picture string.
If a character in the field does not match the picture string format defined
for that field:
1. It replaces any "problem" characters with a space character when it does not match the picture string.
2. The character that has been replaced with a space will be set to a low confidence.
3. Any alternative recognition characters are removed from the field after execution.
Note: This Action is recursive and will affect all child fields of the calling node. If called
on a page object, then all of the fields attached to the page will be processed. If called on
a document object, then all pages in the document will have their fields processed. If called
at the batch level, then all fields within the batch will be processed.
FilterPictureFields
replaces non-matching characters with low confidence spaces,
FormatPictureFields
just lowers the confidence and replaces characters with alternative text, if it is available.
While not direct input to this action, this action works with picture strings
that are defined for each field. The picture string must be set in a DCO variable for
the field object and the variable must be named "PictureString".
If the variable is defined, then the field's data
will be adjusted based on the picture string. If the variable does not exist or is empty,
then the field will not be processed.
rrSet("XxN","@F.PictureString")
FilterPictureFields()
This example expects the rule is attached to a field and that the current field
must have the first character be either a alphabetic character or a digit,
the second character can be an alphabetic character, digit or punctuation character and the remaining characters
must only be digits.
This example also sets the picture string at runtime
by first calling rrSet for the current DCO object then the FilterPictureFields action.
If FilterPictureFields action is called on a page, document or batch level, then
the PictureString variable must first be set on each field to be validated.
Typically this would be set in the SetupDCO for each field at application design time
in Datacap Studio.
method.ret:
Always
True.
The return value does not reflect if fields have passed or failed validation. This action
can operate on multiple fields with a single call, determined by the parent DCO object that
is associated with the ruleset that contains this action. This action will process all of child
fields and update the field text and confidence values based on the picture string as described in the details section.
The results will be shown to the user in a verification panel and can be acted on by subsequent
actions on a field by field basis.
method.see:
Refer to the top-level help topic for the list of available picture character
identifiers that can be used to create a picture string.

method.name: FormatPictureFields
method.ap: None.
method.h:
Uses a picture string to validate the text in a field.
Replaces a character and adjusts the confidence based on the "PictureString" variable defined for the field.
Before calling this action, the variable "PictureString" must be defined in the DCO node for the field
which will be used for validating the field. The variable
can be defined for the node in the Setup DCO or set at runtime using an action like rrSet.
This action Lowers the confidence rating of any character in a field that does not satisfy the criteria
specified in the "PictureString" variable. The picture string used to validate each field is not provided
to this action and instead must be defined in the PictureString variable. This allows each field
to have a unique picture string.
This action adjusts the character confidence of a field, and optionally replaces characters, based on the picture string
that has been set for the field. It is very similar to the
FilterPictureFields
action.
If a character in the field does not match the picture string format defined
for that field:
1. It replaces any "problem" characters with an alternative character from a
secondary recognition engine if one exists. If an alternative recognition character does
not exist, then the original character is left unchanged.
Note: When using alternative text, there must be an equal number of
alternative characters as the field length, and
the alternative character must also be valid within the field's picture string for
substitution to occur. If the alternative recognition character is also not a valid
picture string character, then no substitution will occur.
Additionally, the alternate text must have spaces and punctuation
in the same location as the primary text. For example, if there is a space in the
second position of the primary field text, then the alternate text must also have
a space in this location. If the alternate text does not meet this requirement,
then none of the characters in the alternate text will be use to substitute characters
in the field's primary text.
2. It lowers the Confidence Rating of any character in a field that does not
satisfy the picture string's criteria.
3. Alternative recognition characters are removed from the field after execution.
Note: This Action is recursive and will affect all child fields of the calling node. If called
on a page object, then all of the fields attached to the page will be processed. If called on
a document object, then all pages in the document will have their fields processed. If called
at the batch level, then all fields within the batch will be processed.
FilterPictureFields
replaces non-matching characters with low confidence spaces,
FormatPictureFields
just lowers the confidence and replaces characters with alternative text, if it is available.
While not direct input to this action, this action works with picture strings
that are defined for each field. The picture string must be set in a DCO variable for
the field object and the variable must be named "PictureString".
If the variable is defined, then the field's data
will be adjusted based on the picture string. If the variable does not exist or is empty,
then the field will not be processed.
rrSet("AN","@F.PictureString")
FormatPictureFields()
This example expects the rule is attached to a field and that the current field
must have the first character be an alphabetic character or a space,
the second character must be digit and the remaining characters, if any,
must only be digits.
This example also sets the picture string at runtime
by first calling rrSet for the current DCO object then the FilterPictureFields action.
If FilterPictureFields action is called on a page, document or batch level, then
the PictureString variable must first be set on each field to be validated.
Typically this would be set in the SetupDCO for each field at application design time
in Datacap Studio.
method.ret:
Always
True.
The return value does not reflect if fields have passed or failed validation. This action
can operate on multiple fields with a single call, determined by the parent DCO object that
is associated with the ruleset that contains this action. This action will process all of child
fields and update the field text and confidence values based on the picture string as described in the details section.
The results will be shown to the user in a verification panel and can be acted on by subsequent
actions on a field by field basis.
method.see:
Refer to the top-level help topic for the list of available picture character
identifiers that can be used to create a picture string.

method.name: SetPictureCharacters
method.ap:
PictureID:
The picture string identifier. This must be a digit between 0 through 9.
ValidCharacters:
A string of characters to associate with the picture string identifier.
Smart parameters are supported for all parameters.
method.h:
Configures application specific picture strings assigned to a picture character identifier.
In addition to the predefined character strings, custom picture strings can be configured and then
used in the actions that validate picture strings. The picture character identifier of
"0" through "9" can be configured to allow validations that are not covered by the predefined identifiers.
It is possible to configure your verify panel edit control to restrict keyboard entry based on picture strings
when you use the 'PictureString' field variable. Note that only predefined picture strings work with
the edit control. Any custom picture strings created by SetPictureCharacaters action will not cause the edit control
to restrict user input.
SetPictureCharacters("0","01")
SetPictureCharacters("1","0123")
SetPictureCharacters("2","-./")
ApplyPictureString("0N21N2NN")
This example first creates custom picture strings for picture character identifiers "0", "1" and "2" that
have sets of allowed characters that are not available in the predefined character identifiers.
They are then used in the ApplyPictureString action to provide
tighter control on the allowed input. "0N21N2NN" format matches a typical 6 digit date specification
like "01/07/67". The first character must be only a 0 or 1. The second character can be any number,
the third character must be a standard date separator "-", "." or "/", etc.
Note that a value such as "01/07/1967" would also pass this test because if the field is longer than
the picture string, the last identifier will be used on all remaining characters. Likewise, "01/07/1967123"
would also pass the test. This can be further validated by using length restrictions on the field
using the text length validation actions in the ValidationsAndTextAdjustments action library.
SetPictureCharacters("0","01")
SetPictureCharacters("1","0123")
SetPictureCharacters("2","-./")
ValidatePictureField()
This example is the same as the one above it, the difference is that the picture string has
been setup in the PictureString variable in Datacap Studio, so it is not seen here.
The action ValidatePictureField will then use the custom patterns to validate text
depending on the specification in the PictureString variable in each field object.
method.see:
Refer to the top-level help topic for the list of available picture character
identifiers that can be used to create a picture string.

method.name: ValidatePictureField
method.ap: None.
method.h:
Checks the value of all characters in a field against that field's PictureString criteria.
The DCO variable PictureString must exist in the current fields DCO node. The variable
can be set at runtime or in the SetupDCO as discussed in the top-level help of
this action library.
If a character in the field does not match the picture string format defined
for that field, it lowers the Confidence Rating of any character in a field that does not
satisfy the Picture String's criteria.
Note: Fields with a status of '-1' (Hidden) are checked but this action will not return false if
the value does not match the picture string criteria.
While not direct input parameters to this action, this action works with picture strings
that are defined for a field in the DCO variable PictureString. The predefined picture
character identifiers are described in the top-level help of this action library.
Custom picture identifiers can also be defined using the
SetPictureCharacters
action.
If the validation fails, this action will set the "MESSAGE" variable of the current field with
a failure message. Verify panels will display this message to the user when the field
is visited to give them information as to why the validation failed.
ValidatePictureField()
This example assumes that the field already has the PictureString
variable set on the current field object. Assuming the PictureString
variable is set to "NfAAZ", then these would be the return values
of this action based on the following field values.
"Hello" returns false
"8.0000" returns false
"8.Hello" returns true
"8." returns false
"88Rocket" returns true
method.ret:
False
if the field value does not satisfy the field's Picture String criteria.
Otherwise
True.
method.see:
Refer to the top-level help topic for the list of available picture character
identifiers that can be used to create a picture string.

com.qi: : Actions that help control application logic within rulesets
com.h:
The RuleRunnerLogic action library consists of actions that help control the logic flow
of application rules, actions that move data from object to object and
other batch utility features. These actions
are fundamental actions and every Datacap application is going to use one or
more of these actions in the application's rules.
Do not confuse this action library with the RuleRunner process itself. The RuleRunner process
is a background process that runs Datacap application rules.
Those rules can contain actions from
the RuleRunnerLogic action library, but it does not mean they are exclusively for
the RuleRunner process. Rules can be run by several different Datacap clients
such as DCDesktop, FastDoc, Datacap Studio and any other mechanism that runs
rules within Datacap. The RuleRunnerLogic actions can be used with any
Datacap process that runs rules and they can be used in any application.
⟸ ♕ Datacap Ruleset Overview ♕ ⟹
The Datacap engine performs the steps laid out by the workflow, tasks and rules of
an application. The following are descriptions of these components.
Ruleset: A ruleset is a collection of rules. A single application can contain many rulesets.
A ruleset can contain one or more rules. A ruleset is assigned to one or more Task Profiles.
Rule: A rule is a set of functions that
are associated with one or more DCO objects. (Refer to the ApplicationObjects
top-level help for information about the Datacap DCO hierarchy.) A Rule
can contain one or more functions.
Function: A function can contain one or more actions. Each action will run
one after the other as long as the action returns true. If the last action
in a function returns true, then the rule finishes and no additional actions
are run in the rule. The ruleset will be considered to have a
successful status. If any action in a ruleset returns false, then
no further actions in that function will run. Control will move to the
next function in the ruleset and the actions in the next function
will begin executing. If an action returns false and there are no additional
functions, then the rule will stop and be considered a failed ruleset.
The following shows a generic layout of a ruleset as seen in Datacap Studio:
Ruleset
- Rule
- - Function
- - - Action
- - - Action
- - Function
- - - Action
- - Function
- - - Action
- - - Action
- Rule
- - Function
- - - Action
- - - Action
- - - Action
- - Function
- - - Action
- - Function
- - - Action
The text appearing in the Ruleset, Rule and Function nodes can be
anything that an application developer wants. Often it helps to make
the nodes descriptive, making the intent of the rule or function clear
to anyone looking at the ruleset. Meaningful information will make it
easier when revisiting an application at a later time.
For example, a rule could be named "Other Rule" to indicate that these are
the actions that will be run on the page type "Other". Likewise,
"Invoice Page" could be the name of a rule that is attached to a page type
of "Invoice". Using meaningful text in Datacap Studio for the names of
the Ruleset, Rule and Function tree nodes will make it easier to understand
the logic of the application and to make changes at a later time.
The orders of the rulesets and rules are changeable. Changing the order of
a Ruleset or Rule will not change when the object is run. The order of execution is dependent
on the task profile configuration and the objects that exist at runtime.
Organizing Rulesets and Rules so they appear in execution order within Datacap Studio is recommended
as it will make it easier to understand the rule logic and easier to
debug an application.
The order of the Functions is very important. The first function in a rule
is always run first. The second function will be run only if one of the actions
in the first rule returns false. The third function in a rule will only be run if
one of the actions in the second function returns false, and so on.
The following is an example ruleset for illustration:
MyVerificationRuleset
- My Page Rule
- - Function Load Zone Locations
- - - SetDirectoryFPX("@APPPATH(fingerprint)" name="StrParam")
- - - ReadZonesFPX()
- - - RecognizePageFieldsOCR_A()
- Invoice Field Rule
- - Function Verify Invoice Number Exists
- - - IsTextLength("@X", "1", "˃=")
- - - rrSet("@X","@P.TheValueRead")
- - Function Invoice Number Was Not Read
- - - rrSet("Ooops","@P.TheValueRead")
In the above example, the Rule "My Page Rule" would be attached to one or more page
objects in the Setup DCO. For example, it may be attached to a page type called "Invoice".
The page invoice would have some expected fields, perhaps called "InvoiceNumber".
When the rules engine processes each page object of type "Invoice", it will run the rules
in "My Page Rule" on the object. There could be one page called Invoice or there could
be many pages. Each one will be called, one after the other. The rules first setup
the directory for the FPXML fingerprints location. It then calls ReadZonesFPX which
will load the positions of each field as determined by the associated fingerprint.
These positions indicate the rectangular section on the image that correspond to
each field. The action RecognizePageFieldsOCR_A then uses the OCR_A engine to perform
text recognition for each field on the page. There are many different ways recognition
can be performed such as field level, full page and partial page. It all depends on the needs
of the application. This example happens to use field level which is a very common method.
Once the page rule has completed, then the rules engine will start processing each child object
on the current page, running any rule in the same ruleset that is associated with a field.
In our example, there is just one field associated. It is the InvoiceNumber field which
is attached to the "Invoice Field Rule". The first thing run is the IsTextLength action.
It checks the value of "@X". "@X" means the current object. When no other specification is provided,
"@X" will default to the "Text" value of the current object. In this case, it will grab the
recognized text for the field. It then checks to see if the length of that text is greater
than or equal to 1 character. If so, then it will set a variable on the parent page
object called "TheValueRead". The current field value is copied to the parent page
and stored in the variable "TheValueRead". This is just an example to show a small amount
of what could be done, it isn't something a typical application would do. Many application's rules
would simply perform a validation check and stop, setting the status of the object to 0 or 1, indicating
if it is a "OK" value or a "Failed" value.
If the field did not read any text, then IsTextLength will return false. All subsequent
actions in the function will be skipped. Control will then change to the next function.
In this example, the function "Function Invoice Number Was Not Read" will run, calling
rrSet("Ooops","@P.TheValueRead"), which again will set a variable on the parent page
called "TheValueRead", only this time it will be set to the value "Ooops". Again, this is
just an illustration, the rules could do any number of steps that are required for
an application's use cases.
An action that returns false is not always an undesirable situation
as it is often useful to help control the logic flow.
The action GoToNextFunction
is an action that always returns false. This is useful to force a function
to pass control to the next function. It can allow functions to segregate work
into smaller units broken up logically by functions.
One example could be an instance where actions are needed to perform a task,
but under normal operation, the action may sometimes return false. However,
it is desired to still have the rule continue to do additional work. In this example,
assume that there are four fields on a page that need to have the status
set to Hidden. However, sometimes all the fields may exist, or sometimes only some
may exist, and other times perhaps none of them exist. This could be handled using
a logic flow like this:
Ruleset
- MyPageRule
- - Function Set Field1
- - - rrSet("-1","@P\Field1.STATUS")
- - - GoToNextFunction()
- - Function Set Field2
- - - rrSet("-1","@P\Field2.STATUS")
- - - GoToNextFunction()
- - Function Set Field3
- - - rrSet("-1","@P\Field3.STATUS")
- - - GoToNextFunction()
- - Function Set Field4
- - - rrSet("-1","@P\Field4.STATUS")
- - - GoToNextFunction()
- - Function Stop
- - - SetReturnValue("True")
The above rule will first attempt to set Field1
to a STATUS of -1, which means it is hidden. If the
field exists, the rrSet action will run, then
the action GoToNextFunction will pass control
to the next function. If Field1 does not exist,
rrSet for Field1 will return false. This again will pass control to
the next function which will attempt to set the status for Field2,
and so on for the rest of the desired fields. The last function
calls the action SetReturnValue. This action simply returns True or False
based on the input parameter. Here it returns True, which causes the entire
rule to exit with a "True" or "successful" state.
⟸ ♕ Workflows and Tasks ♕ ⟹
The workflow defines the steps that occur in processing. Each step in the workflow is called
a Task. A workflow can contain any number of tasks. A typical workflow looks similar to this:
Physical Scan or Virtual Scan > PageID > Profiler > Verify > Export
These are the logical steps of the workflow. Often, the number of physical tasks directly map to the logical
steps. That is not a requirement. There can be any number of tasks within the workflow. For example,
the Profiler step could be multiple tasks that segregate the work. Likewise, there may be several
tasks that together comprise the complete Export step.
The PageID task has the actions and steps that determine the type of each ingested document. There are many
different ways this can be achieved, based on the use cases of the application. It can be fully automated
or it can be performed with user interaction.
The Profiler task is a general name for the task that performs the processing of the data in the batch.
It can perform page recognition, call out to databases, perform transactions to third party systems, etc., anything
that is required to get the data extracted, prepared and validated. This task is sometimes separated into
multiple tasks. The benefit of adding more tasks can help spread out processing and makes debugging problems
and maintenance easier.
The Verify task is an interactive user task. In this step, a user would correct verification errors such
as fields that do not meet requirements. For example, a date is not a valid date, an account number is not
a valid account number, a page has not been signed, etc. This task can be skipped if no validation errors
are encountered or if the step is not needed.
The Export task is the logical point where the results of the batch are saved. Files and data can be
copied to other directories, uploaded to repositories, sent to external databases, or any combination of
events. Frequently the export task is actually two tasks, "PreExport" and "Export". Again, the task can be split
into any number of tasks that makes sense for the application.
In addition to the tasks in the workflow, batches can branch or be split into child batches.
When you use branching to route workflows, the entire batch is sent from the main job to a child job.
When the child job completes, the batch returns to the main job.
When you use splitting to route workflows, documents in the batch are split off from the parent batch and
placed into one or more child batches. The child batches are sent to a child job for processing and do not return to the main job.
For branching, use the TaskRaiseCondition action to raise the condition flag of the task.
Branch:
When a task finishes with a Branch condition raised, the Datacap Server creates a new queue record,
and routes the batch to the child job (Fixup). The original parent queue record gets the status as Waiting.
The Waiting status means that the processing is suspended on that workflow until the branch workflow finishes successfully.
In the TravelDocs Fixup example, after an operator reorganizes or rescans the documents and pages into an acceptable sequence,
the Fixup queue status becomes Job Done, and the Main Job picks up processing of the batch where it left off.
Jump:
When a task finishes with a Jump condition, the Datacap Server moves the batch forward or
backwards in the existing job workflow by one or more steps, possibly skipping or re-doing some tasks
within the workflow.
Split:
When a task finishes with the Split condition, the Datacap Server creates new child batches,
as many as the application specifies, each with its own BatchID, batch record, and queue record.
The original parent batch might continue to the next task in the workflow if any documents remain.
The SplitBatch action encapsulates the functionality that is needed to prepare each child batch.
Stop (or not set):
When a task finishes with the Stop condition,
the Datacap Server sets the queue status to Stopped, and no further action is taken.
The "Profile" tab in Datacap Studio is the location that shows each of the rulesets that are run for each profile task
in the workflow. When a task runs, the rule engine will process each of the rulesets listed in
the profile for the task. Rules can be added or changed within the profile as necessary for the application.
⟸ ♕ Custom User Validation Messages ♕ ⟹
The Datacap client validation panel displays fields to a user, highlighting the fields that fail
validation parameters. For example, if a field should be a date, but the date format is not valid, that
will be highlighted and a message will be displayed to the user when the field is selected. Another example
could be that a field must be at least 5 characters long but cannot be more than 10 characters long, a failure
of the validation test will cause the field to show as a problem to the verify operator and display a message
that is associated with the failed field.
The DCO can contain two special variables, MESSAGE and MessageID. These variables are used by actions
and clients to convey information to the user as to why a field has a failed validation test. Many of the
validation actions in the ValdiationAndTextAdjustments action library will automatically set this variable
to display pre-translated messages to the user.
It is possible that an application may require additional
validation tests with messages that are custom to the application, created by the
application developer. An application can be written to
display custom messages to the user within the verification panel using the actions
MessageSetTextAndID, MessageSetRuntimeParameter, MessageClear and MessageSetText. If required,
translated versions of these messages can be also displayed, based on the
current language displayed for the client application. It would be up to the application developer
to acquire translations of their custom messages.
To allow translated messages, the messages must be defined in a file called resources.json.
The default language file must be placed in the "Project" directory of the application.
This is the directory with the "dco_" prefix. For example, for the application APT, the
project directory is APT\dco_APT. The default language resources.json file must be in that
directory. Translated versions of this file must be placed in subdirectories named using the standard
language identifier. For example, the French translation would be placed into APT\dco_APT\fr,
the German translation would be placed into APT\dco_APT\de, the Brazilian Portuguese
translation would be placed into APT\doc_APT\pt-br, etc.
The action MessageSetTextAndID must be used to set the message and it will be looked up
at runtime by the client application in the appropriate language file. Optionally, the action
MessageSetRuntimeParameter can be used to populate replacement parameters at runtime, and the values
of these parameters can also be optionally translated.
The file resources.json is not required if messages do not require translation.
The json file uses entries of this format: "keytype.keyid":"value". Key-value pairs are
separated by commas and usually placed one per line for ease of reading and update.
The "keytype", must be one of these values: "job", "task", "shortcut", "field", "workflow",
"appname", "pagetype", "doctype", "text", or "variable". The "keyid" is user defined.
Example json file:
{
"workflow.TravelDocs":"Travel Documents",
"field.Airfare":"Airfare",
"field.Taxes":"Taxes",
"field.Unit_Cost":"Unit cost",
"field.Total":"Total cost",
"message.M001":"Invalid car type selected. Enter {0}, {1}, {2}, {3} or {4}."
}
If some text should not be translated, then it is recommended to not place it in the json file
to prevent accidental translation.
The message to display from the resources.json file is configured using the MessageSetTextAndID action
and, optionally, the MessageSetRuntimeParameter action. Refer to the help for these actions for
details.
⟸ ♕ Smart Parameters - Reference Guide ♕ ⟹
If an action supports smart parameters, it is specified in the action help of the action. Smart parameters are very powerful
specifications for action parameters that allow access of data to and from other DCO objects and perform
special pre-defined operations in one step.
Smart parameters can be used to dynamically obtain or create action input parameters at runtime. For example,
an action could be provided the value of a field after recognition, a parameter could pull the value from a
DCO variable that was set by a previous action, or a smart parameter could evaluate to the current date, the current
time, the current job ID, the current operator ID, the path to the current batch that is running, and more.
Smart parameter syntax can also be used to build expressions at runtime that concatenate dynamic data and
static data at runtime. Smart parameters are
a flexible way to provide a wide range of input to any action that supports smart parameters.
Smart Parameters Object Hierarchy Navigation
One of the abilities of smart parameters is the syntax to specify which DCO object to access when
reading or writing a variable. For example, a rule runs on a particular DCO object, but may need to access
information from a different object.
For example, an action on a page object may need to test, copy or set a value on a child field object
and smart parameters are the method to accomplish this task.
To better understand the Datacap Object Hierarchy, see information provided
in the top-level help of the ApplicationObjects action library.
Not all actions support smart parameters. Check the action help to confirm if smart parameters are supported.
If an action supports smart parameters, it can also mean that certain hard coded values need to be specifically
escaped or specified to have them interpreted as desired.
@B.VariableName
Accesses the value of the specified variable on batch DCO node, regardless of the current DCO node level.
The current DCO node does not need to be batch level.
The current node can be a batch, document, page or field node and this syntax accesses the parent batch node.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the value of the TYPE variable for the batch.
The second example creates a new variable Name at the batch level and sets the value to “Fred”.
rrGet("@B.TYPE")
Result: rrGet is typically called on a field node. The value "TravelDocs" is then set on the field text value.
rrSet(“Fred”,”@B.Name”)
Creates the variable "Name" at the batch level and sets its value to “Fred”. This value can then be used in a subsequent action
called on the same DCO node, or any DCO node.
@D.VariableName
Accesses the value of the specified variable on a document level DCO node.
The current DCO node does not need to be a document level node. The current node can be a document, page or field node and this syntax accesses the parent document node.
If the current level was Document, then the current DCO node would be accessed.
If the action is called from a page or field, then the parent document node would be used, provided
the hierarchy does have a parent Document node, which is the typical case.
For example, the "other" page type is atypical in that respect because not have a parent Document node.
This syntax should not be used on a batch level DCO node.
In the first example, the smart parameter obtains the value of the TYPE variable for the current document
and compares it to an expected type. In the second example, a value is set on the document node.
rrCompare("@D.TYPE", "Car_Rental")
Result: If the document type matches "Car_Rental", the action returns true, otherwise it returns false.
rrSet(“Hotel_Rental”, “@D.ImportantInfo”)
Result: The action creates a variable on the document node called "ImporantInfo" and sets it to "Hotel_Rental".
The source variable could also be a smart parameter and pull the value from another location,
such as from a field value.
@P.VariableName
Accesses the value of the specified variable on the current, or parent, page DCO node.
If the current node is a page node, then the current DCO node would be accessed.
If called on a field, this would access the parent page node, assuming it is a standard page structure and the field has a parent page object.
This syntax would not be used on a batch or document DCO node.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the value of the TemplateID variable for the current page.
rrCompare("@P.TemplateID", "1022")
Result: This action uses the system variable "TemplateID" to check the value of the fingerprint assigned to the current page.
@F.VariableName
Accesses the value of the specified variable within a field and would be called on a field DCO node only.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the value of the TYPE variable for the current field.
rrGet("@F.TYPE")
Result: rrGet reads the system TYPE variable for the current field node and put the value, such as "Pickup_Date", into the current
field's text value.
@X.VariableName
Accesses the text of the specified variable on the current node.
This smart parameter enhances the portability of the rules by working generically on the current DCO node.
For example, a function that is written for the page level can be reused at another level by simply tying the
ruleset to a new DCO object without having to update the @X smart variable to the new level. It allows someone
to write a rule without having to worry about the current node level as the syntax works for the current node
at any level.
Uses the current node specifier, @X, when calling an action with a smart parameter.
SplitFileName("@STRING(C:\Dir1\Dir2\MyFile.abc)","@X.FRoot","@X.FPath", "@X.FName","@X.FExt")
Result: This example splits the file and saves the information into 4 variables on the current node:
FRoot = "C:\"
FPath = "C:\Dir1\Dir2"
FName = "MyFile"
FExt = ".abc"
If this action were run a page object, this is an example XML representation of the created variables:
˂P id="TM000001"˃
·· ˂V n="TYPE"˃Other˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="STATUS"˃49˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="IMAGEFILE"˃tm000001.tif˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="PageName"˃tm000001˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="ScanSrcPath"˃C:\Datacap\MyApplication\Images\Input\MyTestImage.tif˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="FRoot"˃C:\˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="FPath"˃C:\Dir1\Dir2˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="FName"˃MyFile˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="FExt"˃.abc˂/V˃
@B\ObjectName[\ObjectName][.VariableName]
Accesses objects in the batch with the navigation starting at the batch level. The @B specification can be called
from any level within the hierarchy and starts the navigation from the batch level.
The first ObjectName specified must be an object that is an immediate child of the batch object.
Additional levels of object navigation can be specified. For a batch level navigation, usually the most common
navigation would be for a field, when there is a field present at the batch level, which is sometimes done
to support specific types of operations. A \document, \document\page, or \document\page\field specification can be
provided. For example, "@B\Invoice\Main_Page\PO_Number" could be specified to navigate down to the field "PO_NUMBER" and access
that object. However, in practice, this is not usually useful as there can be many child documents called "Invoice" on the
batch object. Similarly, there can be many child pages called "Main_Page" off of a document node. In this scenario,
the navigation always select the first child encountered in the hierarchy. For the specification "@B\Invoice\Main_Page\PO_Number",
the first child document encountered matching "Invoice" is be used, next the first page found matching "Main_Page", then the PO_Number
field is accessed. Indexing to other pages of the same name is not possible with this syntax.
This type of specification would typically only be used from the batch level when there is a field
directly attached to the batch object, because there will only be one field for that object and there will be no ambiguity.
The VariableName is optional. If specified, the variable named will be read or written. If not specified, it will
use the "Text" property, which is typically only valid for field objects.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the value of the Text variable for the batch-level field "Field2".
Sample XML representation segment of the DCO showing the batch-level field called "Field2":
˂B type="APT"˃
·· ˂V n="ID"˃0˂/V>
·· ˂V n="TYPE"˃Batch˂/V>
·· ˂V n="STATUS"˃0˂/V>
·· ˂V n="MIN TYPES"˃0˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="MAX TYPES"˃0˂/V˃
·· ˂P type="Other" pos="0" min="0" max="0"/˃
·· ˂D type="Document" pos="0" min="0" max="0"/˃
·· ˂F type="Field2" pos="0" min="0" max="0"/˃
rrCompareCase("@B\Field2", "Car", "False")
Result: Accesses the batch level field called Field2 and if the value of that field is "Car", then the action returns True.
Otherwise the action returns False.
@D\ObjectName[\ObjectName][.VariableName]
Accesses objects in the batch with the navigation starting at the document level. The @D specification can be called
from a document level, or an object level lower than the document level. It cannot be called from a batch level object.
If called from an object lower than the document level, navigation starts from the parent document object.
The first ObjectName specified must be an object that is an immediate child of the current document object.
Additional levels of object navigation can be specified. A \page or \page\field specification can be
provided. For example, "@D\Main_Page\PO_Number" could be specified to navigate down to the field "PO_NUMBER" and access
that object. However, in practice, this is not usually useful as there can be many child pages called "Main_Page" off of a document node. In this senario,
the navigation always selects the first child found in the hierarchy. For the specification "@D\Main_Page\PO_Number",
the first child page found matching the name "Main_Page" is accessed, then the PO_Number
field on that page is accessed. Indexing to other pages of the same name is not possible with this syntax.
The VariableName is optional. If specified, the variable named is read or written. If not specified, the smart parameter evaluates to
the "Text" property, which is valid for field objects only.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the value of the TYPE variable for the field “Field1”, which is directly attached to the current document.
rrSet("@D.STATUS", "@D\Main_Page\PO_Number.STATUS")
Result: This smart parameter navigates down to the first child page called "Main_Page" then navigate to the "PO_Number" field and set it to the same status as the current document node.
If Main_Page cannot be found or if PO_Number cannot be found, a blank value is be set.
@P\ObjectName[\ObjectName][.VariableName]
Accesses objects in the batch with the navigation starting at the page level. The @P specification can be called
from a page level, or lower, object. It cannot be called from a batch level or document level object.
If called from an object below the page level, navigation starts from the parent page object.
The first ObjectName specified must be an object that is an immediate child of the page object.
Additional levels of object navigation can be specified. A \field or \field\field specification can be
provided. For example, "@P\PO_Number" could be specified to navigate down to the field "PO_NUMBER" and access
that object. This allows a page to access the value of a child field.
This syntax is also important as it allows a field to access a sibling field.
For example, if the current DCO node was a field called "Tax", it could also use the syntax "@P\PO_Number"
to access the value or variables from a sibling field on the page called "PO_Number".
The VariableName is optional. If specified, the variable named is read or written. If not specified, smart parameter evaluates
use the "Text" property, which is typically used for field objects only.
Navigation from a page level object down to field level objects is the most common use case because there can only
exist a single child field of a specific name. This is unlike a document or batch object that can have multiple child objects
of the same name at runtime, making the correct navigation ambiguous. The @P\ syntax is also a common way for
fields to access a sibling field.
In the first example, the smart parameter returns the text of the Car_Type field on the current page.
In the second example, the smart parameter returns the value of the TYPE variable of the Car_Type field.
The example assumes this is the field as represented in XML:
˂F id="Car_Type"˃
·· ˂V n="TYPE"˃Car_Type˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="STATUS"˃1˂/V˃
·· ˂C cn="10" cr="588,748,600,769">83˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘S'
·· ˂C cn="10" cr="605,748,620,769">85˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘U'
·· ˂C cn="10" cr="625,748,643,769">86˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘V'
˂/F>
rrSet("@P\Car_Type", "@P.MyCarType)
Result: Creates a variable called "MyCarType" on the page object with the value "SUV"
rrCompare("@P\Car_Type.STATUS", "0")
Result: From the page level rules, it checks the status of the field "Car_Type" and if the status is 0, the engine runs the rules after the
rrCompare action. Because the STATUS is 1, rrCompare returns False and control jumps to the next function within the current ruleset.
@F\ObjectName[\ObjectName][.VariableName]
Accesses objects in the batch with the navigation starting at the field level.
As the field is the lowest level of object, the "F" specification can only be called from a field object.
A field is allowed to have a subfield as a child object. Using the navigation syntax, it is possible to run a rule
on the parent field that accesses the variables in subfield.
The VariableName is optional. If specified, the variable named is read or written. If not specified, it evaluates to
the "Text" property of the field.
In these examples, the rule that contains the action is bound to a field with subfields.
In the first example, the smart parameter returns the text of the Unit_Cost subfield of the current field.
In the second example, the smart parameter returns the value of the Unit_Cost subfield TYPE variable.
For the example, here is an XML representation of the DCO that shows the current field has a subfield called "UnitCost".
˂F id="Other_Charges_Line_Item0"˃
·· ˂V n="TYPE">Other_Charges_Line_Item˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="STATUS"˃0˂/V˃
·· ˂F id="Unit_Cost"˃
···· ˂V n="TYPE"˃Unit_Cost˂/V˃
···· ˂V n="STATUS"˃1˂/V˃
···· ˂C cn="10" cr="1290,511,1305,540">36˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘$'
···· ˂C cn="10" cr="1308,515,1321,536">57˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘9'
···· ˂C cn="10" cr="1325,533,1329,536">46˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘.'
···· ˂C cn="10" cr="1334,515,1348,536">57˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘9'
···· ˂C cn="10" cr="1350,515,1365,536">48˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘0'
·· ˂/F˃
˂/F˃
rrSet("@F\Unit_Cost", "@X")
Result: The value $9.90 from the subfield Unit_Cost is copied to the value of the current field.
rrSet("@F\Unit_Cost.STATUS", "@F.STATUS")
Result: Updates the current field with the status 1 from the subfield "Unit_Cost".
@X\ObjectName[\ObjectName][.VariableName]
Accesses objects in the batch with the navigation starting at the current object level.
The ObjectName must be a child of the current object. If additional ObjectNames are provided,
they must exist under the previously specified object.
For example, if called on a document node, the first ObjectName specified must be an object that is an immediate child of the current document object.
Additional levels of object navigation can be specified. A \page or \page\field specification can be
provided. For example, "@X\Main_Page\PO_Number" could be specified to navigate down to the field "PO_NUMBER" and access
that object when the current node is a document.
However, in practice, this is not usually useful from a document object as there can be many child pages called "Main_Page" off of a document node. In such a situation,
the navigation always selects the first child found in the hierarchy. For the specification "@D\Main_Page\PO_Number",
the first child page of the document object that is found matching "Main_Page" is accessed, then the PO_Number
field on that page is accessed. Indexing to other pages of the same name is not possible with this syntax.
Navigation is usually performed on a page or field object because they can only have single instance of the named object.
The VariableName is optional. If specified, the variable named is read or written. If not specified, the smart parameter evaluates to
the "Text" property, which is typically only valid for field objects.
Navigation from a page level object down to field level objects is the most common use case because
every child field contains a unique name. This is unlike a document or batch object that can have multiple child objects
of the same name at runtime, making the correct navigation ambiguous. If a field object needs data from a sibling field,
then use the @P\ navigation from the field object so the navigation starts from the parent page object.
This example assumes that a page level node is the current object.
In the first example, the smart parameter returns the text of the Car_Type field on the current page.
In the second example, the smart parameter returns the value of the TYPE variable of the Car_Type field.
The example assumes this is the field as represented in XML:
˂F id="Car_Type"˃
·· ˂V n="TYPE"˃Car_Type˂/V˃
·· ˂V n="STATUS"˃1˂/V˃
·· ˂C cn="10" cr="588,748,600,769">83˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘S'
·· ˂C cn="10" cr="605,748,620,769">85˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘U'
·· ˂C cn="10" cr="625,748,643,769">86˂/C˃ ˂-- ‘V'
˂/F>
rrSet("@P\Car_Type", "@P.MyCarType)
Result: Creates a variable called "MyCarType" on the page object with the value "SUV"
rrCompare("@P\Car_Type.STATUS", "0")
Result: From the page level rules, the action checks the status of the field "Car_Type" and if the status is 0, the engine runs the rules that follow the
rrCompare action. Because the STATUS is 1, rrCompare returns False and control jumps to the next function within the current ruleset.
@X\ObjectName[\ObjectName][.CONFIDENCESTRING]
The variable "CONFIDENCESTRING" is a special designation to get and set the confidence of field text.
The each character in a text field has a special confidence attribute. The confidence comes from the recognition engine
and indicates how sure it is that a character was recognized correctly. A confidence of '9', indicates that the engine
was very confident that the character is correct. The lowest confidence of '0' is used to indicate that the engine
is not sure the character is correct. As the value progresses up to '9', the engine becomes more sure that it did a good job
during recognition.
When specifying smart parameter navigation syntax, if the variable specified is "CONFIDENCESTRING" and the syntax
specifies a field, then the operation will get or set the confidence of the text within the field. If CONFIDENCESTRING
is specified on any other kind of node, then it will act as a standard DCO variable.
The specified confidence string can set unique values for each character. Only characters between 0 to 9 are allowed.
If the specified confidence string is shorter than the text in the field, the remaining characters will be given a confidence of '9'.
If the specified confidence string is longer than the text in the field, the extra characters will be truncated.
Only characters 0 through 9 are allowed in a confidence string.
Additional mechanisms can also manipulate the confidence value of a field.
The smart parameter @DCO(CONFIDENCESTRING), allows reading of the confidence, but cannot set the confidence.
The ApplicationObjects action SetFieldConfidence will set the confidence of a field, but it allows only a single
confidence specification and sets all characters in the field to the same confidence.
rrSet("11339", "@F.CONFIDENCESTRING")
This example assumes that the action is run on a field. It sets the confidence for the field to "11339".
rrSet("@P\Field1.CONFIDENECESTRING", "@X.TheFieldConf")
This example assumes that the action is run on a page and the page has an existing field called "Field1".
The confidence of Field1 will be stored into a page level variable called "TheFieldConf".
Smart Parameters Predefined Variables - Application Configuration
@APPPATH(KeyPath)
Retrieves the path to a file or folder from the application's configuration (.app) file.
Use the Datacap Application Manager to modify the information that is contained in this file.
Do not edit the file directly.
Syntax
@APPPATH(KeyPath)
Arguments
KeyPath: Specifies the key within the application configuration file to query.
If the field name is unique within the file, you can specify just the field name.
If the field name is not unique within the file, you must specify the path to the instance you want.
For example, you might have multiple workflows. If you do not specify the path, you get the first instance.
To obtain the path, move the mouse pointer over the field in the Datacap Application Manager and read the path from the tooltip.
You can use @APPPATH to retrieve the following information from the application configuration file.
Field name ············ Key name ·········· Example ········································ Notes
Application fields
Batches folder ········ runtime ············ @APPPATH(runtime) ························ (Field name is unique)
Export folder ·········· export ·············· @APPPATH(export) ·························· (Field name is unique)
Fingerprint folder ····· fingerprint ········· @APPPATH(fingerprint) ····················· (Field name is unique)
Workflow fields
Setup DCO ············· setupdco ·········· @APPPATH(setupdco) ······················ (assumes single workflow)
Rules folder ············· rules ················ @APPPATH(dco_Workflow1/rules) ······ (specifies Workflow 1)
VScan source folder · vscanimagedir ·· @APPPATH(vscanimagedir) ················ (assumes single workflow)
Imagefix INI ·············· imagefix ·········· @APPPATH(dco_Workflow2/imagefix) ·· (specifies Workflow 2)
@APPVAR(KeyPath)
Retrieves a connection string, value, or other attribute from the application configuration (.app) file.
Use the Datacap Application Manager to modify the information that is contained in this file.
Do not edit the file directly. The Datacap Application Manager encrypts the connection strings and decryption is handled by the standard actions.
Attention: Before Datacap 8.0, this parameter returns the value for the specified variable as defined in the [Variables] section in paths.ini.
The .ini file is in the process folder of the application. The application configuration has replaced the paths.ini file in Datacap versions
after 8.0.
Syntax
@APPVAR(KeyPath[:attribute])
Arguments
KeyPath: Specifies the path to field you want. See @APPPATH for details.
attribute - Specifies the attribute name (optional):
For custom values, use "v" (if you do not specify an attribute, "v" is assumed).
For connection strings, use "cs".
The easiest way to get the path and attribute is to look in the Datacap Application Manager:
On the Application and Datacap tabs, move the mouse pointer over the field and read the smart parameter value from the tooltip.
On the Custom Values tab, read the smart parameter value that is displayed in each section.
You can use @APPVAR to retrieve the following information from the application configuration file.

Smart Parameters Predefined Variables - Batch
@BATCHID
Returns the value of the id attribute for the current batch. The batch ID can be useful to save as metadata
with a batch for history and tracking. It can be used for other things such as naming of data files.
In this example, the batch ID and page ID are used to name the export file.
SetExportDirectory("@APPPATH(export)")
SetExportFileName("Export_+@BATCHID+_+@ID+.txt")
Result: When these actions are called on a page node, they use the batch ID and the current page ID to name the export file.
The export file name will be similar to: "Export_20240046.001_TM000001.txt"
@ID
Returns the value of the id attribute for the current object.
For example, if the rule that contains this special variable is bound to a page, the current object is the current page.
In this example, the batch ID and page ID are used to name the export file.
SetExportDirectory("@APPPATH(export)")
SetExportFileName("Export_+@BATCHID+_+@ID+.txt")
Result: When this is called on a page node, the action uses the batch ID and the current page ID to name the export file.
The export file name will be similar to: "Export_20240046.001_TM000001.txt"
@STATUS
Returns the value of the STATUS variable for the current object.
STATUS is also a setup property and might specify a special characteristic (for example,
a status of -1 indicates a hidden field). The @STATUS is logically equivalent to the syntax "@X.STATUS".
The DCO status can be set to any value, however specific values are considered to be a standard and have special uses
in specific actions and verification panels. The list of typical status values is provided in the top-level help
of the ApplicationObjects action library.
In this example, the rule that contains the action is bound to a page and the smart parameter returns the status of the current page.
rrCompare("@STATUS", "1")
Result, if the status of the object is 1, which typically means there is a problem, rrCompare returns true and the next action
is run. For example, perhaps there is some logic that should only be run in the event of a failed page or field, it can be
controlled using this action.
rrSet("0", "@STATUS")
Result: This action sets the current object status to 0, which means there are no problems. Object status can be set explicitly within
rules as needed. Status can also be implicitly changed by verification panels and some actions.
@VALUE
Returns the text of the current object, which is expected to be a field. The "Text" variable of a field is what
holds the field's value. For example, this is where field recognition text is stored and used for display to an end user.
In this example, the rule that contains the action is bound to a field and the smart parameter returns the text of the current field.
If the current object is not a field, @VALUE looks for a value in a variable Text of the calling object.
rrCompareCase("@VALUE", "SUV", "FALSE")
Result: If the field value matches "SUV" in upper or lower characters, then the action rrCompareCase returns True and the next action runs.
Otherwise, the action returns False and skip to the next function in the ruleset.
@VAR(VariableName)
Returns the value of the specified variable on the current object.
The @VAR keyword works logically the same as @X. @X has been adopted as the standard replacement for @VAR
as it logically fits in with the other smart parameter syntax such as @F, @P, etc.
In this example, the rule that contains the action is bound to a page. The smart parameter returns the value of the TYPE variable for the current page.
rrCompare("@VAR(TYPE)", "Rental_Agreement")
Result: If the current page is of type "Rental_Agreement", rrCompare returns True, running the actions that follow.
This allows for special processing when a "Rental_Agreement" page is encountered.
Smart Parameters Predefined Variables - Job / Task
These are predefined smart parameters that have special meaning and are related to obtaining read-only job and task information at runtime.
@JOBID
Returns the ID of the current job. This ID is the value that is specified in the ID field on the Datacap Administrator Workflow tab.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the ID of the current job.
rrCompare("@JOBID", "MainJob")
Result: Obtains the current job ID and compares it to "MainJob". If it matches exactly, it returns True, otherwise it returns False.
This could be useful to change the application rule flow based on the name of the job.
@JOBNAME
Returns the name of the current job. This name is the value that is specified in the Description field on the Datacap Administrator Workflow tab.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the name of the current job.
rrCompare("@JOBNAME", "MainJob")
Result: This action obtains the current job name and compares it to "MainJob". If the current job ID matches exactly,
it returns True, otherwise it returns False.
This is useful to change the application rule flow based on the name of the job.
@OPERATOR
Returns the user name of the person who ran the job.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the name of the person who ran the job.
rrSet("@OPERATOR", @X.TheOperator)
Result: This action obtains the name of the current operator and stores it into another variable on the current object. One possible use could be to pick up
this variable later and store it as metadata with a batch to keep track of the operator that ran the batch.
@STATION
Returns the ID of the station that runs the job. This ID is the value that is specified in the ID field on the Datacap Administrator Workflow tab.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the ID of the station that runs the current job.
rrSet("@STATION", @X.TheStation)
Result: The action obtains the name of the current station, such as station "1", and stores it into another variable called "TheStation".
One of the uses of this action is to pick up
this variable for later and store it as metadata with a batch to keep track of the station that ran the batch.
An alternative example use could be to perform an rrCompare or rrCompareNot and perform special rules based on the station.
@TASKID
Returns the ID of the current task. This ID is the value that is specified in the ID field on the Datacap Administrator Workflow tab.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the ID of the current task.
rrCompare("@TASKID", "Export")
Result: Obtains the current task name and compares it to "Export". If it matches exactly, it returns True, otherwise it returns False.
This kind of test could be useful to change the application rule flow based on the name of the job.
@TASKNAME
Returns the name of the current task. This name is the value that is specified in the Description field on the Datacap Administrator Workflow tab.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the name of the current task.
rrCompare("@TASKNAME", "Export")
Result: This action obtains the current task name and compares it to "Export". If the taskname matches exactly, it returns True, otherwise it returns False.
This kind of test is useful to change the application rule flow based on the name of the job.
Smart Parameters Predefined Variables - Utility
These are predefined smart parameters that have special meaning and are related to obtaining read-only information at runtime.
The items in this section are of general use.
@CHR(UnicodeValue)
Returns the character corresponding to the specified decimal Unicode value. This can be particularly useful for passing
a parameter value that is also a smart parameter special character, allowing it to be passed to the action as the indicated
character value without additional smart parameter processing on the character, such as slashes, plus signs and the "at" symbol.
It is also useful to pass a value that may be
difficult to type into the edit field of Datacap Studio but still needs to be passed to an action.
In this example, the smart parameter returns the @ character corresponding to the value 64. This is an example
of testing a field value to a hard coded expected value that contains an @ symbol.
rrCompare("Hi+@CHR(64)+There", @F)
Result: The parameter @CHR(64) resolves to "@". The + signs cause this value
to be concatenated with the text before and after it, resulting in the string "Hi@There". The rrCompare action
then compares that string to the text value of the current field. If the string matches, the action returns true,
otherwise it returns false.
This is an additional example to show that the CHR can be used multiple times in a parameter.
rrCompare("Hi+@CHR(64)+There+@CHR(33)", @F)
Result: The value stored in the current text value for the field is "Hi@There!".
@DATE(Format)
Returns the current date in the format specified.
If Format is blank, the default format is “MM/DD/YYYY”.
The Format specification allows the representation to be customized to the date value meets a required format.
Valid date formats are:
“yyyy-MM-dd”
“yyyy/MM/dd”
“MM-dd-yyyy”
“MM/dd/yyyy”
Note: You can reformat a date field by calling the ValidationsAndTextAdjustments action IsFieldDateWithReformat function on the current field.
i.e. IsFieldDateWithReformat("yyyy/MM/dd")
In this example, the smart parameter returns the current date.
rrSet("@DATE(mm.dd.yyyy)", @X.CurrentDate)
Result: The current date, in a format like 12.31.2024, is stored in the current object with a variable called "CurrentDate".
That variable can be accessed later as needed. For example, it may be stored with the batch as metadata.
@DCO(PropertyName)
Returns the value of the specified DCO object property for the current object.
The DCO object is an internal data structure that contains the current runtime batch hierarchy information.
For more information on the DCO, refer to the top-level help of the ApplicationObjects action library.
Supported PropertyName values:
"ID": The ID of the current DCO node.
"TYPE": The type of the current DCO node.
"STATUS": The status of the current DCO node.
"IMAGENAME": The file name for the current image. Valid on a Page DCO object.
"TEXT": The text for the current DCO node. Valid on a Field DCO object.
"CONFIDENCESTRING": A string representing the confidence values for each character in the text value of the field. Valid when called on on a Field object only.
"XML": The XML representation of the DCO.
In this example, the rule that contains the action is bound to a page.
The example also contains the smart parameter returns the portion of the runtime batch hierarchy XML for the current page.
rrSet("@DCO(ID)", "@X.MyVar")
Result: The ID of the current object is placed into a variable named "MyVar".
@DICT_VALUE(field)
This special variable works with OMR fields (indicated by the value RecogType=4) that are bound to a dictionary.
It returns the dictionary values corresponding to the items that are selected in the specified OMR field.
In this example, the rule that contains the rrGet action is bound to a page that contains an OMR field (Options).
The OMR field has three subfields and is bound to the dictionary shown in the XML code.
On the current page all three options are selected, so the return string contains all three dictionary values.
rrGet("@DICT_VALUE(Options)")
Result: Navigation System Child Seat Fuel Service
This assumes the following OMR setup:
˂DICT n="Options"˃
˂W v="Navigation System"˃Navigation System˂/W˃
˂W v="Child Seat"˃Child Seat˂/W˃
˂W v="Fuel Service"˃Fuel Service˂/W˃
˂/DICT˃
@DICT_WORD(field)
Same as @DICT_VALUE, except this special variable returns the dictionary words corresponding to the selected items.
@DICT_VINDEX(csv_string)
This special variable works with actions bound to an OMR field (RecogType=4) where the OMR field is bound to a dictionary.
The parameter returns a string of 1's and 0's corresponding to the dictionary values you specify as a comma-separated list.
In this example, the rule that contains the rrGet action is bound to an OMR field.
The OMR field has three subfields and is bound to the dictionary shown on the right.
The values that are specified correspond to the second and third items in the dictionary, so the return value is 011.
The rrGet sets the character values on the three OMR subfields to 0, 1, and 1.
rrGet("@DICT_VINDEX(Fuel Service,Child Seat)")
Result: The value 011 is set on the current field, assuming the OMR is setup as follows and the last two items are checked.
˂DICT n="Options"˃
˂W v="Nav System"˃Nav System˂/W˃
˂W v="Child Seat"˃Child Seat˂/W˃
˂W v="Fuel Service"˃Fuel Service˂/W˃
˂/DICT˃
@EMPTY
This special variable represents an empty string. This smart parameter is often handy to explicitly represent an empty string
instead of passing a simple empty quote. There can also be a situation where this variable is the only possible way to correctly
pass an empty string to an action that supports smart parameters.
In this example, rrSet clears the custom page variable MyVar.
rrSet("@EMPTY","@P.MyVar")
This example checks to see if a DCO variable is empty. If the variable is empty, or does not exist, the action returns True.
rrCompare("@EMPTY", "@X.message")
@PILOT(PropertyName)
Returns the value of the specified Pilot object property.
The Pilot object is an internal data structure that is configured by Datacap at the start of task execution.
It contains the information that is required to run the task. Such as the batch folder (BATCHDIR),
the batch ID (BATCHID), the input DCO file (DCOFILE), the task priority (PRIORITY).
Allowed PropertyName values:
"BATCHID": The current batch ID. i.e. "20240101.00000".
"BATCHDIR": The full path to the current batch directory. i.e. "C:\Datacap\Application\Batches\Sample.00000".
"OPERATOR": The current operator.
"STATION": The current station.
"CHILDRENQUANTITY": The children count, dependent on the DCO object.
"PROJECTPATH": The path to the application's DCO directory. i.e. "C:\Datacap\Application\Application_DCO".
"PAGESINBATCH": The number of pages in the batch, dependent on the DCO object.
"DOCSINBATCH": The number of pages in the batch, dependent on the DCO object.
"EXPECTEDPAGES": The number of pages in the batch, dependent on the DCO object.
"ADJUSTEDPAGES": The number of pages in the batch, dependent on the DCO object.
"ADJUSTEDDOCS": The number of pages in the batch, dependent on the DCO object.
"JOBNAME": The current job name.
"DCOFILE": The path to the current DCO. i.e. C:\Datacap\TravelDocs\batches\20230004.004\Export.xml. At runtime the DCO is in memory so the file on disk will not reflect the current state.
"JOBID": The current job ID.
"TASKID": The current task ID.
Assuming this action is called on a page object, this example takes the image file associated with
the page and copies it to a file with the same name as the original page with the new extension ".backup.tif".
CopyFile("@VAR(IMAGEFILE)", "@PILOT(BATCHDIR)+\+@ID+.backup.tif", true)
In this example, the smart parameter returns the input DCO file for the current task.
rrGet("PILOT(DCOFILE)")
Result: Gets the path to the current DCO file and writes it to the current field. This assumes the action rrGet was called on a field object.
@PROCESSDIR
Returns the full path to the dco_˂app_name˃ folder of the application.
An example of populating a field value with the process directory.
rrGet("@PROCESSDIR")
Result: Assuming this is called on a field object, the field value is updated with the path to the DCO directory. i.e. C:\Datacap\TravelDocs\dco_TravelDocs
@STRING(Text)
Returns the value that is specified as a string. The STRING directive allows hard coded
text to be passed as a parameter to an action without the text being interpreted as a smart parameter.
While this is not required for most text, if the hardcoded input text contains smart parameter special characters
such as slashes, @, +, and ., then this prevents them from being interpreted.
The @STRING specification must meet one of the following specifications:
The ending parenthesis must be a parenthesis followed by a plus sign, such as "@STRING(stuff)+".
The ending parenthesis must be the last character in the parameter.
